concepts.name: Appointment of the Prime Minister: conventions, discretion and membership of Parliament
concepts.description: Article 75, the convention of the majority leader, presidential discretion, proof of majority and membership of the Houses.
concepts.idea: The President appoints the Prime Minister, but conventions bind the choice except where discretion arises.
concepts.rule: Article 75 says only that the President appoints the Prime Minister; by convention the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha is appointed. When no party has a clear majority, or the Prime Minister dies suddenly with no obvious successor, the President may use personal discretion (Charan Singh, 1979; Rajiv Gandhi, 1984), but must appoint the leader whom the ruling party elects. The Delhi High Court (1980) held that a majority need not be proved before appointment, and the Supreme Court (1996) allowed a non-member to be Prime Minister for six months. The Prime Minister may belong to either House, whereas in Britain the Prime Minister must be in the House of Commons.
concepts.example: Charan Singh (1979) was appointed as coalition leader and then asked to prove his majority.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the appointment of the Prime Minister:

1. Article 75 says only that the Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President; it lays down no specific procedure for selection.
2. Article 75 itself requires the President to appoint the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha as Prime Minister.
3. When no party has a clear majority, the Prime Minister so appointed is usually asked to seek a vote of confidence in the House within a month.

questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: Article 75(1) says only that the Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President and lays down no selection procedure. Statement 2 is incorrect: the practice of appointing the majority-party leader comes from the conventions of the parliamentary system, not from Article 75 itself. Statement 3 is correct: when no party has a clear majority, the person appointed is usually asked to seek a vote of confidence in the House within a month.

concepts.name: Oath, term and salary of the Prime Minister
concepts.description: The oaths of office and secrecy, the pleasure of the President, loss of Lok Sabha confidence and the Prime Minister's pay.
concepts.idea: The Prime Minister takes two oaths, has no fixed term and is paid as Parliament determines.
concepts.rule: The President administers the oaths of office and secrecy before the Prime Minister enters office; the oath of office has four undertakings and the form is similar to that of any Union minister. The term is not fixed and the Prime Minister holds office during the pleasure of the President, but cannot be dismissed while enjoying majority support in the Lok Sabha. On losing its confidence the Prime Minister must resign or can be dismissed (V.P. Singh 1990, Deve Gowda 1997). Salary and allowances are determined by Parliament; the Prime Minister gets those of an MP plus a sumptuary allowance, free accommodation, travelling allowance and medical facilities.
concepts.example: V.P. Singh resigned in 1990 after defeat in the Lok Sabha.

concepts.name: Powers of the Prime Minister over the council of ministers and other roles
concepts.description: Recommending and removing ministers, portfolios, presiding, collapse of the council, and the chairmanships and other functions.
concepts.idea: The Prime Minister heads the council: it is formed on his or her recommendation and falls with his or her resignation or death.
concepts.rule: The Prime Minister recommends the persons the President may appoint as ministers, allocates and reshuffles portfolios, and can ask a minister to resign or advise the President to dismiss him or her. He or she presides over the council, guides and coordinates all ministers, and can bring about its collapse by resigning. The resignation or death of the Prime Minister dissolves the council (in practice the outgoing council is usually asked to continue until a successor is sworn in); that of any other minister merely creates a vacancy. The Prime Minister chairs NITI Aayog (which succeeded the Planning Commission), the National Integration Council, the Inter-State Council and the National Water Resources Council, shapes foreign policy, is chief spokesman, political-level crisis manager, party leader and political head of the services.
concepts.example: A Prime Minister who differs with a minister can ask for his resignation or advise the President to dismiss him.

concepts.idea: The Prime Minister links the President with the council and advises, rather than acts, in matters of Parliament and appointments.

concepts.description: What Morley, Harcourt, Jennings, Laski, Greaves, Munro, Crossman, Berkely and Ambedkar said of the Prime Minister.
concepts.idea: Writers on Britain describe the Prime Minister as a dominant figure, and the same holds good in India.
concepts.rule: Lord Morley called the Prime Minister 'primus inter pares' and 'key stone of the cabinet arch', holding a position of exceptional and peculiar authority. questions.e: Under Article 75(1) the President appoints the other ministers on the advice of the Prime Minister; the Prime Minister allocates and reshuffles portfolios, can ask a minister to resign, and the resignation or death of the Prime Minister dissolves the council, which does not happen with any other minister. So the Prime Minister holds authority beyond that of colleagues.
w: The President is bound by the advice of the council under Article 74, so the Prime Minister is not a nominal head.
Collective responsibility binds the council together but does not equalise authority; only the Prime Minister can reshuffle portfolios or recommend dissolution.
The resignation of a single minister only creates a vacancy; the council is dissolved only by the Prime Minister's resignation or death.

concepts.name: Chief Ministers who became Prime Ministers and the caretaker government
concepts.description: The six Chief Ministers who became Prime Ministers and the meaning, limits and precedents of a caretaker government.
concepts.idea: The Constitution does not provide for a caretaker government, which may manage routine business only.
concepts.rule: Six people (Morarji Desai, Charan Singh, V.P. Singh, P.V. Narasimha Rao, H.D. Deve Gowda and Narendra Modi) became Prime Ministers after being Chief Ministers; Desai was the first non-Congress Prime Minister (March 1977) and Rao the first from South India. The Constitution contains no provision for a caretaker government; the term describes a council that has lost confidence or been dissolved but is asked to continue. It manages routine business and makes no significant policy decisions except on national security or interest. The Tarkunde Committee (1974-75), the communique of President Reddy (August 1979) and the Calcutta High Court (December 1979) support these limits.
concepts.example: After the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the outgoing council cannot launch major new schemes.

provides for it in Article 74, limiting it to the routine administration of the Government of India
provides for it in Article 75, for a maximum of six months after the dissolution of the Lok Sabha
provides for it only after the Rajya Sabha has been dissolved and the Lok Sabha has completed its term

questions.e: The Tarkunde Committee (1974-75), an unofficial committee appointed by Jayaprakash Narayan, made these recommendations on caretaker governments.

Rejected: Statement-I is correct; a caretaker government is expected to avoid significant decisions.
